content.html: Sneezing, itchy eyes, or a stuffy nose getting in your way? Visit your local Unichem or Life Pharmacy.

From antihistamines, nasal sprays, and eye drops to expert advice, our pharmacists can recommend the right option to help you feel better. Not sure what’s triggering your symptoms? We have simple tips to help you manage allergens this season.
While you’re in store, it’s also a great time to get your flu vaccination and stay protected as flu season approaches.

Imminent means pollen production for this plant type is expected to begin within the next 2 weeks.

High means high levels of pollen production. These pollens are in the air and are highly likely to cause more severe inhalant allergy in sensitised persons.

Moderate means the pollen types are in the air and are likely to cause significant inhalant allergy in sensitised persons.

Low means that although the plant mentioned is releasing pollen, little pollen is being released or the type of allergen does not spread widely.

modules.title: Airborne Allergen Forecast for Christchurch Central

content.text: About 25 – 30% of our population is allergic to one or more allergens – with those allergic to inhaled pollens being the greatest group. These allergic particles are carried on the air, and come from plants which are flowering. Particles from sporing fungi both inside our houses and outside, from pets, from bedding and from other sources also contribute.

Pollen is shed from flowering plants as microscopic grains 15 to 50 micrometres across. Pollens are allergenic because the air-borne grains release proteins upon contact with water, which allows the pollen to fertilise the receiving plant.  It is these proteins which may cause an allergic reaction if you are sensitised.
Pollen grains from wind-dispersed plants are very light and buoyant and can travel long distances. Only when they are shed in large numbers are they visible as dust or as a cloud in the air.

Although there is localised pollen production in the winter months of May and June from some cypress and cedar trees, the main full pollen season runs from July through to February and March of the following year. The season varies slightly in its timings each year depending largely on plant growth and development in the preceding year, for that is when much pollen formation is initiated, and on the weather, especially temperature, experienced in the late winter and spring.

Dramatic pollen production and air-distribution begins in July or August with the Pinus (pine) season. This is seen by everyone as yellow dust which settles on car surfaces, and rings around puddles, ponds and lakes. Other early pollen hazards here are wattle (Acacia) where pollen is shed in polyads or larger clusters, macrocarpa (Cupressus macrocarpa -pollen of which has been shown to sensitise up to 30% of asthma clinic attendees in Melbourne) and hazelnut (Corylus) a potent allergenic pollen which may have an occupational implication here as the emerging horticultural industry grows. This continues into August/September and overlaps with deciduous trees like oaks, elm, birches, alders, poplars and ash - all potent aeroallergens to persons sensitised to them.

The major pollen hazard in New Zealand, the grasses, dominate in October through to and after Christmas and finally olive trees, privets and chenopod/amaranth/composite weeds contribute to pollen load in January and February. Fungal spores are produced into the air in February and March but are there in all months. Spores, and danders (dried saliva) from pets, house dust mites from inside bedding all contribute to ‘hayfever’. Asthma can be exacerbated by all or some of these inhaled allergens.
Adapted from content provided by Dr David Fountain, Associate Professor in Plant Biology, Massey University.
